implementation_notes: The suspend modifier is language-level, but the asynchronous invocation primitives live in the kotlinx.coroutines library, so the pattern arrives as a library: async { } starts a coroutine and returns Deferred<T> - a Job that also carries a value - and await() is the collect step, suspending rather than blocking until the value is available or the exception is rethrown. Structured concurrency replaces the manual ownership bookkeeping: async is a CoroutineScope extension, so coroutineScope { } guarantees that children are joined and that a failure cancels the siblings, supervisorScope opts out only where isolation is intended, and awaitAll/select collect several deferred values. The dispatcher (Dispatchers.Default/IO/Main) is the pattern's executor, and delay is genuinely non-blocking, so tens of thousands of outstanding calls cost far less than a thread each. Hand-rolled handle/callback structures are never needed; the only justified bridge is JVM interop, where a java.util.concurrent API demands a Future (future { } and asDeferred()/asFuture adapt both directions) - and even there the sanctioned shape is to keep suspend functions to the boundary and convert once.
pitfalls: GlobalScope.async opts out of structured concurrency: a failure of the caller no longer cancels the task and an orphaned Deferred can leak - own the coroutine in a scope tied to the caller's lifecycle.

A Deferred that is never awaited still reports failure through its parent scope (or stores it until await in a supervisor scope); CoroutineExceptionHandler is not a substitute for observing a Deferred. For intentional fire-and-forget use launch in an owned scope with an explicit error handler, or keep and await the Deferred.
Dispatchers.Default is sized for CPU work: blocking calls (JDBC, file I/O, sleep) must move to Dispatchers.IO or they starve the pool.
Cancellation is cooperative - the coroutine must reach a suspension point or check isActive, otherwise it runs to completion regardless of the cancel call.

Blocking primitives (Thread.sleep, runBlocking inside a coroutine, or a synchronous lock held across a suspension) negate the benefit and can deadlock a single-threaded dispatcher; use suspending APIs and release locks before suspension.
